video_title: Where Is The Crypto Alpha Hiding This Cycle?
gist: Panel of crypto allocators (Arthur of Defiance Capital, Rajiv of Framework Ventures, Smac of Compound) argue this cycle rewards fundamentals and selection: high dispersion has most liquid funds beating BTC/ETH, consensus names like Hyperliquid keep outperforming, and long-short works on both legs. Crypto-AI is maturing via Nous Research, Venice AI and GPU financing (USDAI), while AI cuts startup capital intensity and seed looks less crowded than late-stage.

themes.theme: Crypto x AI: where it is finally real

insights.claim: Arthur says crypto-AI went through a 2023 phase of 'false fitting' but over the past year legitimate projects emerged, citing Nous Research as builder of Hermes, which he calls the largest open-source AI agent framework.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Crypto-AI has moved from narrative to credible teams; Nous Research is a reference name for the sector.
insights.quote: There was a lot of false fitting of a crypto and AI theme. But I think over the past 1 year, we start to see more and more things that make sense.

insights.claim: Venice AI, described as a privacy-focused crypto version of OpenRouter for routing inference, still has far less token spend than OpenRouter but a hockey-stick growth chart, per Arthur.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Privacy-routed inference is a live, growing crypto-AI revenue niche worth tracking vs OpenRouter volumes.
insights.quote: the token spend and inference is still not as big, but the growth chart is still like hockey stick

insights.claim: Rajiv argues crypto's strongest AI angle is capital formation for the AI capex buildout; Framework portfolio company USDAI does mid-market GPU cluster financing (e.g. $150M of GPUs) at more attractive rates with smaller down payments than alternatives.
insights.speaker: Rajiv (Framework Ventures)
insights.so_what: On-chain GPU-backed credit is a concrete crypto-AI use case tied to AI capex demand.
insights.quote: One of our portfolio company, USDAI, is doing like mid-market cluster financing.

insights.claim: Smac contends crypto-AI should not try to compete with centralized AI on efficiency today; its edge is permissionlessness, coordination, alternative economic models and pushback against centralized frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Smac (Compound)
insights.so_what: Underwrite crypto-AI on coordination/permissionless wedges, not cost/performance parity.
insights.quote: if crypto AI is going to compete on efficiency today, that's probably not the place that makes the most sense.

insights.claim: Arthur argues crypto-AI projects enforce encryption and privacy by default unlike mainstream AI, and as the world cares more about privacy it will find the solutions already exist in crypto-AI.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Privacy demand in AI is a potential tailwind for crypto-native AI stacks.

insights.claim: The machine-to-machine payments case for crypto-AI rests on whether blockchains can push per-transaction cost below the floor centralized card rails impose, which Smac calls still TBD.
insights.speaker: Smac (Compound)
insights.so_what: Agent payments thesis hinges on unit cost vs card rails; watch for real cost-competitive volume.
insights.quote: can we smush the actual cost of doing this towards a level that's more competitive that a centralized provider can't compete with?

insights.claim: Rajiv floats that agent swarms needing durable, available messaging could use permissionless ledgers or persistent storage, suggesting someone crawl Arweave or Filecoin to see if agent swarms already use them.
insights.speaker: Rajiv (Framework Ventures)
insights.so_what: On-chain data from storage networks could reveal early agent-swarm demand ahead of consensus.
insights.quote: crawl, um, Arweave or Filecoin and see if like, uh, any of these agent swarms are already using it today

insights.claim: Arthur argues that if an AI agent goes rogue it will use crypto rather than a bank or fintech API because of permissionlessness, making the crypto-agent combination powerful but with unforeseeable outcomes; still too early to call.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Permissionless rails are the default for autonomous agents, implying both demand and security/exploit risk.
insights.quote: if a AI agent go rogue, is it going to use a bank API or a fintech API? It's going to use crypto.

insights.claim: Smac notes a shift toward local/smaller models and distributed inference aligns with crypto's ideals, but whether crypto projects capture value there remains an open question.
insights.speaker: Smac (Compound)
insights.so_what: Value capture, not narrative fit, is the key diligence question for decentralized inference tokens.
insights.quote: the value capture is always like an open question with a lot of these things

insights.claim: Arthur says liquidity is not a real obstacle to accumulating a few percent of any protocol over time with modern execution tools unless a fund exceeds roughly $500M-$1B AUM.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Liquid token funds below ~$500M can size into illiquid names; capacity constraint bites above that.
insights.quote: I don't think it's a really an issue except if you are like more than 500 million or billion dollars and above.

insights.claim: Defiance budgets for 5-10% variance in final entry (and exit) price when building positions, treating ~5% slippage as an acceptable cost, since venture also underwrites volatility but simply doesn't mark it daily.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Practical sizing rule for liquid-venture: accept ~5% slippage rather than trying to time entries.
insights.quote: if you're okay to pay 5% slippages, you shouldn't really have an issue building a position.

insights.claim: Rajiv says sizing is harder now because teams may not OTC and crowding is higher: funds do similar homework, so things become consensus quickly and prices move fast once a thesis is recognized.
insights.speaker: Rajiv (Framework Ventures)
insights.so_what: Edge decays faster; first-mover entry matters more in liquid crypto.
insights.quote: There's also a lot more crowding these days in the market where things become consensus a little bit more quickly

insights.claim: Compound shifted from only pre-seed/seed (4-5 deals a year) toward liquid tokens because it wasn't meeting enough founders to say yes to and wanted exposure, believing there are more investable liquid assets than 5-10 years ago, while avoiding levered-beta exposure.
insights.speaker: Smac (Compound)
insights.so_what: Venture funds migrating to liquid books adds a new class of fundamental buyers to mid-caps.
insights.quote: it can just turn into a a levered beta asset class, which is um yeah, which is like kind of not as interesting to us.

insights.claim: Arthur claims more than 80% of crypto liquid/hedge funds he knows are outperforming BTC and ETH this year, with most up 20-100% year-to-date while BTC and ETH are down year-to-date.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Dispersion is high: selection is paying while majors lag, favoring active managers over beta.
insights.quote: most of the crypto funds I know is like up like from 20 to 100%

insights.claim: Arthur argues Hyperliquid (HYPE) shows consensus among smart money no longer means a top: it has been consensus for over a year, is a large-cap, and keeps outperforming because of fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Don't fade strong-fundamental consensus names by default; fundamentals now drive price more than positioning.
insights.quote: just because an asset is consensus among a smart money doesn't mean it can't outperform anymore

insights.claim: Arthur describes a bifurcation: retail chasing 10-20x has moved to micro-cap memecoins ($100k-$50M caps), while size players congregate in majors or fundamentally strong mid-caps.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Mid-cap fundamental names compete for institutional flows; retail froth sits in memecoins rather than alts.

insights.claim: Smac says crypto theses play out in 3-6 months, much faster than equities, so investors must pre-define exit conditions and model who the marginal buyer will be after them.
insights.speaker: Smac (Compound)
insights.so_what: Shorter thesis half-life requires starter positions, fast sizing, and explicit exit triggers.
insights.quote: you have to also at least try to think about or model out who like who will be the marginal buyer of the things that I'm buying today.

insights.claim: Rajiv says positions that look crowded short-term can be less consensus over a longer horizon, so time horizon and entry timing are the main tools for managing crowding.
insights.speaker: Rajiv (Framework Ventures)
insights.so_what: Longer holding periods can sidestep short-term crowding in consensus names.

insights.claim: Arthur calls this the golden age of long-short in both crypto and equities: shorts in failing projects near shutdown can drop ~50% every six months, and cross-asset pairs (long equity/short crypto or vice versa) work as fundamentals trend.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Short legs in dying tokens are now alpha sources, not just hedges.
insights.quote: you can actually make money both on a long leg and a short leg because there are some projects are really not making it

insights.claim: Arthur cites the 'treasury' trade (a reference to crypto treasury plays) as an example where technically oversold assets kept falling because fundamental drivers overpowered positioning.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Don't buy oversold signals against strong fundamental downtrends.
insights.quote: nobody expected the treasury to like keep dropping

insights.claim: Arthur says Bitcoin remains the benchmark most LPs care about, alongside absolute returns, since indices like CCI30 or the Bloomberg crypto index never gained popularity.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Fund performance will be judged vs BTC; alt-heavy books must beat it to raise capital.
insights.quote: Both absolute returns and Bitcoin outperformance, yeah. That's the only two things people care about in my view.

insights.claim: Smac argues spot ETFs like IBIT make BTC a bare-minimum baseline, since an LP can buy IBIT directly, and suggests crypto might eventually be benchmarked against deep-tech equities or tech indices.
insights.speaker: Smac (Compound)
insights.so_what: ETF access raises the bar for active crypto funds' fee justification.
insights.quote: if I'm an LP and I can go buy IBIT for example, like why why what's the point of allocating to um like a a fund that doesn't outperform that.

themes.theme: Venture: seed vs growth and AI-lean startups

insights.claim: Arthur observes extreme overlap among late-stage deals in equity and crypto because so few happen, while seed has a lot of opportunity because everyone got burned, though AI is pulling away quality founders.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Late-stage crypto rounds are crowded; seed is less competitive but founder supply is thin.
insights.quote: I think seed stage is a lot of opportunity right now, because everyone got so burned.

insights.claim: Arthur says crypto and AI are probably the only sectors where a well-chosen seed investment can return ~50x within one to two years.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Fast convexity keeps capital flowing to crypto/AI seed.
insights.quote: I don't know whether any other industry you can get like a 50x in like two years

insights.claim: As a liquid-only fund, Defiance would ideally hold 10-20 names but is usually restricted to 5-10 because the investable universe is small, so more seed activity that leads to tokens benefits it.
insights.speaker: Arthur (Defiance Capital)
insights.so_what: Liquid investable universe remains narrow, concentrating flows into few quality tokens.
insights.quote: I think the ideal portfolio size for us is like 10 to 20 names, but usually we are just restricted to five to 10 names.

insights.claim: Rajiv says seed-stage founder count has fallen versus 2-3 years ago after right-sizing, but the number of outlier founders hasn't, and growth-stage companies now have durable traction rather than narrative, likely drawing generalist growth funds into crypto.
insights.speaker: Rajiv (Framework Ventures)
insights.so_what: Expect non-crypto growth generalists to enter later-stage crypto rounds, supporting valuations of proven protocols.
insights.quote: there will be uh additional market participants maybe who aren't even really in crypto and and maybe more more of the growth generalist funds

insights.claim: Smac is optimistic that crypto sectors written off after failing 3-5 years ago may work now with the right founder and timing, as crypto becomes a less low-status industry relative to AI.
insights.speaker: Smac (Compound)
insights.so_what: Revisit 'dead' crypto sectors; timing, not concept, may have been the failure.
insights.quote: a world in which that was not the right time to try some of these things three, four, five years ago.

insights.claim: AI has lowered early-stage crypto capital intensity: portfolio companies operate with fewer employees, keep AI-native staff, and headcount budget is being reallocated to compute and API credits, so a $10M raise goes much further unless training models.
insights.speaker: Smac (Compound)
insights.so_what: Smaller rounds can reach milestones; lower dilution and fewer follow-on needs for crypto startups.
insights.quote: A meaningful chunk of that head count is probably being reallocated to compute or API credits and stuff like that.
